The essential instrument of that control appears in clause 26 which we are now discussing. Although there may be many other important provisions in regard to publication, the most essential provision of all is the establishment of a scrutiny committee of Parliament to assert its control over delegated legislation.
It is true, as the minister indicated, that a resolution will be put before the House by the House leader dealing with the setting up of a scrutiny committee. But what I like about the first of the amendments is that it provides that a scrutiny committee shall be established before the coming into force of this legislation for the purpose of reviewing and scrutinizing statutory instruments. I think it is as well that the statute make this provision because in my view the legislation without the committee is like Hamlet without the Prince of Denmark. The legislation would be inadequate. I think it should spell out that the two procedures, namely, the setting up by the House or by the Senate of the scrutiny committee and the enactment and bringing into force of this legislation are concurrent procedures-and they have my approval.
When he dealt with the powers of the committee, the minister said: Let the House determine by its rules what the powers of the committee shall be. I agree with the minister that many of the powers of the committee and many details of the committee's operations are rightly left to the rules of the House. But what the amendment is dealing with is not the details of the committee's operations but the fundamental function of the committee. It gives the committee not only the power to look at the statutory instruments that are referred to it; it explicitly gives the committee power to recommend that the same be approved, varied or repealed.
I think the minister pointed out that this power may be implied, that it may already exist under the rules of the House. I would ask him this question: Why should it not be enacted by a statute that in effect creates this statutory instruments regulation, and which incidentally I think should provide for the scrutiny committee to inspect and to regulate? I think the power to recommend that statutory instruments be approved, varied or repealed should be included in the legislation in order to establish the supremacy of Parliament. I think we are not dealing here with a minor matter but with a question of basic principle, namely, the supremacy of Parliament.
It is because I think the amendments make this clear- if they do not establish it-that I am in favour of the amendments. If amendment No. 3 is not passed, then my remarks will be the same on the fourth amendment and I will give it my support if it comes before the House.

Mr. Speaker, I hope you will be as indulgent with me as you were with previous speakers and will allow me to make some general observations on the two motions now before us. If Your Honour does that, I promise, when my turn comes to present my motion, not to be repetitive and to put my argument succinctly.
First may I make some observations and say what I hope the committee on regulations, or the scrutiny committee as it is called, will do. Recommendation 19(1) says that the committee should be a standing committee of the House of Commons. I hope that it will be a committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons, partly for the reason advanced by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), namely, that it would have continuity. Certain members of that committee would not need to worry about the quadrennial bugle call and rumpus of an election campaign and could keep their minds at all times on the regulations and other statutory instruments that the committee must scrutinize. As I say, they would serve on it continuously. Others of us might not be able to. The Senate members could be working when the rest of us were out on the hustings. They could be scrutinizing the regulations. For that reason I hope the committee is set up as a joint committee.
The second recommendation with which I thoroughly agree is the one saying that all regulations should stand permanently referred to the committee. My third and final point about the committee is that I hope its procedure will be flexible enough so that any member who is faced with a problem concerning any regulation can immediately take his doubts or his problem to the committee for immediate advice. Perhaps there would be longer range scrutiny of the matter.
If I could mention an experience of mine, perhaps it would bring the message home to the minister. Last year or the year before the Department of Fisheries passed some pretty stringent regulations which affected the rights of people to hold lobster fishing licences, to pass the title of a boat to other people or to hold that title in partnership with other people, and the like. This created a fair amount of correspondence with fishermen in the Halifax area. Sometimes one can be overwhelmed by a flood of letters and become unable to give proper advice. That is something I was faced with. If there had been a committee to which was attached a specialist, much like the Auditor General who helps the members of the Public Accounts Committee, it would have been a great help. I do not know what one should call such an official. Should one call him, perhaps, the scrutineer general, or the statutory instruments general?

The hon. member suggests that he be called the statutory ombudsman. This place is throbbing with suggestions. I merely said that there should be a permanent functionary who should help this scrutiny committee. The points that appeal most to me are that the committee be a committee of both Houses, that all

March 8, 1971

regulations stand permanently referred to it, for reasons I shall elaborate on in a few minutes, and that any member should feel that it is his right to take to that committee any problem that comes in his morning's mail, and that the committee with the help of the grand inquisitor or the statutory ombudsman will get to work immediately.
May I now refer to the points raised by the hon. member for Peace River and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). From the minister's remarks I had considerable difficulty in deciding if the bill went far enough or if it should have more teeth in it. Perhaps I could best illustrate my difficulty by quoting the evidence found in volume No. 7 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, of Tuesday, February 16, 1971. At that time we were considering the bill. Before the committee were the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) and Mr. P. D. Beseau of the legislation section of the Department of Justice. I raised the matter originally in the way that is found at the bottom of page 9. I asked:
The other question deals with the remedy, should a regulation or statutory instrument be found offensive in some regard. I take it that that committee reviews and scrutinizes it, but I am wondering whether we should not spell out a specific remedy in case the committee finds it wanting.
The Minister of Justice replied:
Mr. Chairman, this enters, of course, into the relationship of the executive and the legislature. The executive is responsible for the preparation and issuance of regulations. We are providing through this bill a system whereby all regulations subject to certain narrowly drawn exceptions are published and sent to the scrutiny committee. The scrutiny committee will be a committee of Parliament. Parliament will have the recourse of drawing it to the attention of the executive by any means ordinarily available to Parliament, much in the way of the Public Accounts Committee or any other committee of the House.
That exchange ought to make us suspicious, because the Public Accounts Committee comes to this House almost every year with 20 or 30 recommendations. In any event, it comes in with a lot of flack. We sometimes hear complaints from the members of the committee that not all their suggestions are acted upon. I do not suppose all the recommendations of any committee can be acted upon; nevertheless, it seems to me that this procedure does not leave the members of the Public Accounts Committee as happy as they otherwise might be.
The following exchange also took place in the committee:
Mb. McCleave: We do get a report in which a committee has Identified what it thinks is wrong about it but it seems to me that we should be taking it one step further to provide for it to be immediately or within 15 days brought for a discussion and a vote by either house of Parlement.
Mb. Tubneb (Ottawa-Cableton) : Could that not be left to the rules of the House and the resolution of the scrutiny committee as to how Parliament is to deal with it? We did not want to circumscribe how Parliament should act in this statute.
Mb. McCleave: I would be inclined to accept that but my colleague says no so perhaps I should throw it to him.

My colleague the hon. member for Edmonton West continued the discussion. Later, as found on page 26, that clause was stood at my request until I had had a chance to study it. After walking up and down the hall and talking to a few people about this, because I was concerned in case we were not developing an effective procedure, the following exchange took place:
Mb. McCleave: Mr. Chairman, I have had some discussion with my colleagues on this side about it and it seems to me that the right to make regulations is permanently referred to the committee to be established. So the committee can report to either Chamber that the regulation is excessive, unjust, or the like. This not only puts government on notice at that time, but there is no reason that the committee cannot next week come back and say the same thing, and say it over and over again, because the act is always there before the committee. A report on it does not render the committee functus with regard to that particular act or the regulation passed under it. I think in that respect we have a greater safeguard than the Alf Hales-
Instead of "act" I should have said that the regulations are there before the committee. The exchange continued as follows:
Mb. Tubneb (Ottawa-Cableton) : Public Accounts.
Mb. McCleave: Yes. In that respect we have, because they can become functus on something but the committee never could as I read it.
The minister then said:
The general umbrella is created by statute but it is un to either House to supplement it and put it through.
I said:
But subject to perhaps stumbling on some better procedure I would be happy to accept it. I withdraw my objection.
Perhaps I am to be commended for that bit of caution at the end. Where I said there might be a better procedure on which we might stumble.
May I repeat the issue as I see it. The minister agreed that the regulation would always be before the committee and the committee could report on that regulation. It could report one week and, if the government took no action, presumably it could report the next week, and so on, if it felt very strongly what it regarded as an injustice in the regulation. The danger is that it depends on whether the committee is established as an independent committee; in other words, it will not be pushed around by anyone. If it were exercised enough, it could report to either House time and again. My remedy is fine in one respect, but not if the committee does not feel encouraged to always report on its difficulties.
The proposals of the hon. member for Edmonton West and the hon. member for Peace River do not state that the committee has the final say as to whether the regulation is defective. That is very important. It would be most improper to give any committee of this House the right to substitute its opinion for that of a government department with its expertise, the Governor in Council, the cabinet and their advisers. That would be wrong; also, it would be constitutionally unsound. However, I think the committee does have a right to express an

March 8, 1971
Statutory Instruments Act
opinion and to make a recommendation based on that opinion.
With the resources, expertise and common sense of the collective members, I think the committee has a right to report to this or the other chamber on any matter that has been referred to it. For example, they have the right to say that they have examined the regulations under the beekeepers act and feel that in some respects they are unjust and offend some of the rules laid down in the accepted Parliamentary practices of the world and, more particularly, the rules set forth in paragraph 7 (a-j) of the report of the statutory instruments committee. That opinion could then be tested. That is the real crunch in the whole issue.
I do not apologize for going into this matter at some length because I think we may reach a consensus. The minister is a fair man; he will listen to us. When the President of the Privy Council (Mr. McEachen) brings in legislation to set up the committee, many of the issues may already have been cleared out of the way. I do not apologize for scouting it at some length. Either remedy in the amendment before us seems to be very useful. The remedy suggested by the hon. member for Peace River, as contained in subclause 3, reads;
Where a statutory instrument stands referred to such committee, the committee has, in respect of such statutory instrument, the power to recommend that the same be approved, varied or repealed.
That does not say "the power to approve, vary or repeal." It is simply a power to make the committee's opinion or recommendation known to the House. I think that is important. Again, we are not substituting a decision for that of someone else. We are simply stating whether we regard what has been done by the regulation-making authority is proper. It is up to Parliament to decide. No doubt the government, with all its abilities, will not have great difficulty if we are not on the right track. If we are on the right track, the regulation will probably be very quickly amended and the remedy secured without having to go to the House for a vote.
The other remedy, suggested by the hon. member for Edmonton West, is a little more complicated. It is set out in subclause 3 as follows:
In the event that the said committee should in any report recommend the amendment, replacement or annulment of any statutory instrument such report shall be brought on for consideration in the House of Commons within fifteen sitting days after the tabling thereof in the same session, if such be possible, or within the first twenty sitting days in the next session following and any debate thereon shall continue subject to the Standing Orders of the House of Commons, until the report shall have been finally disposed of.
Again there is no attempt by the committee to substitute its decision for that reached by the minister, the Governor in Council or whoever has the power to make regulations. It is simply a right to comment on whether it regards the exercise of those powers to have been carried out properly, and to report to the House to have the procedure clearly spelled out so that all members can state whether they think the regulatory power has been
properly exercised. Those are the main points. That is why I recommend either one of these two courses.
It is about half a minute to 10 o'clock. I understand that one member of the New Democratic Party, who is not present this evening, would like to speak on this matter. I also understand that the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) would like to say a few words on the subject. Perhaps the House would permit these hon. members to speak later on this important subject.

CONSUMER AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF SPREAD IN PORK PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 22, which seems quite a while ago, I addressed the following question to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford):
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. In view of the spread in pork prices between the 20 cents a pound for dressed pork which a farmer receives in Saskatchewan and the retail price of pork products such as ham, which sells for $1.20 per pound, will the minister look into this price difference and consider appropriate action?
Mr. Speaker, since farming began, farmers have been concerned about the fact that their bargaining position has not always been as good as it should have been. They hope that their bargaining position and their share of the consumers' dollar can be improved. I should like to address a series of questions to the minister or to the parliamentary secretary. First, I would ask him to look at this question and tell the House what action he is contemplating in connection with this wide disparity between the amount farmers receive and the amount consumers are paying. Does the Minister of Consumer Affairs concern himself about the difference in prices

March 8, 1971

received by primary producers and those paid by consumers? Does he consider he has any place in this equation?
What check does he or his department make to find out whether someone is applying pressure in the marketplace? Is there a continuous check to see whether someone is applying undue pressure on the price of a product or a service, in this case the price of pork? Does he keep any consistent watch, if you will, to find out whether pressure is being applied? Does the minister concern himself about price wars which the supermarket chains may be waging among themselves in the course of which they force consumer prices down and then insist on reducing payments to producers of red meat?
I suggest this is the case. In the committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs during an examination of Bill C-181 I asked one of the witnesses whether this was the case. He replied that those engaged in the meat industry naturally tried to get a fair price for their products but when there was a supermarket war in progress the supermarkets put pressure on the meat packers to reduce their prices and pass the reduction on to the producers. In what way is the department concerned with these things?
Does the Department of Consumer Affairs concern itself at all with the relative difference in the bargaining position as between one group and another in the marketplace, or does it just make out as best it can? Does it attempt to judge the price margin on different products, in this case pork, or is the position of the ministry merely one of pricing can sizes, comparing weight units, acting as watchdog over advertising, and so on? I am suggesting to the parliamentary secretary that the department should really get down to the meat of the matter-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the production of hogs in 1970 has only been exceeded in one earlier year, as the hon. member may know, and that was in 1944. A combination of ample feed grains in the west and high prices in 1969 led to a large increase in output, and during the latter half of 1970 the price of hogs declined dramatically. The national average price was $34.63 in 1969 and this had fallen to $22.94 in the first week of January, 1971. These prices refer to 100 pounds dressed weight. These statistics are quite important and relevant.
There have been significant declines in the price of retail pork cuts. Ham, smoked boneless, dropped from an average of $1.35 per pound in 1969 to $1.14 in December, 1970. Shoulder roasts, Boston butt, fresh, fell from 73.5 cents in 1969 to 56.6 cents in December, 1970. These are national averages compiled by DBS. The relation between hog prices and the price of retail pork products was examined in detail by the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Consumer Credit and Prices, I think in the fall of 1966. The conclusion of the committee was that there was no simple relationship between the price of hogs and individual retail cuts. One thing did emerge clearly. A high level of consumer demand for a particular cut such as hams will mean that its price will not rise or fall in the same way as the price of the whole carcass. I hope this will clarify the situation, Mr. Speaker.
